KEY MESSAGE 1...

Lingering lake effect clouds will gradually  decrease heading into 
this evening and overnight. A few high level cirrus clouds could 
arrive late tonight, otherwise it will be clear and cold with high 
pressure overhead. Temperatures tonight will dip down into the upper 
10s to lower 20s over the region. Wednesday will feature mainly 
sunny skies, with some late day thin high cirrus clouds arriving 
from the south. Light east-south east winds develop through the day, 
under 5 MPH and temperatures reach near average levels for late 
November (in the 40s). It looks to remain dry even Wednesday night 
just ahead of the in coming coastal storm. Clouds increase, lower 
and thicken through the night. Cold overnight lows are expected once 
again, in the upper 10s to mid-20s. Easterly winds gradually 
increase through the night, especially over the hilltops.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

A robust 996 MB coastal low will move north through eastern North 
Carolina and toward Chesapeake Bay on Thanksgiving Day. This 
surface low is supported by a large, negatively tilted 500mb trough, 
which eventually closes off into an upper level low over the 
Tennessee Valley region on Thursday. A strong easterly low level jet 
will develop off the Atlantic ahead of the coastal low, with 850mb 
winds progged to be at 75-85kts over the eastern portion of the 
forecast area Thursday afternoon. This is around 3 standard 
deviations above normal, and also transports plenty of moisture into 
the area as well, with PWATs also 2-3 standard deviations above 
normal for this time of year (1.25 inches).

Rain will overspread the area from south to north, moving across 
Northeast PA between about 9 AM and Noon. The rain looks to 
overspread the Southern Tier during the midday to early afternoon 
hours, then the rest of Central NY during the mid to late afternoon 
hours. Thermal profiles support generally a cold rain from this 
system on Thanksgiving Day, but can't rule out a few ice pellets or 
very patchy and brief freezing rain over the highest elevations
(above 2000 feet) in the Poconos and (above 2500 feet) in the 
Catskills at the immediate onset of the precipitation. No 
meaningful accumulations of ice or snow are expected across our 
entire forecast area. Periods of rain continue into Thursday 
evening, before a possible dry slot moves in Thursday night. 
Rainfall totals between 0.75 to 1.50 inches are expected across 
the forecast area. Considering the dry antecedent conditions 
this fall across the region, this rainfall is not expected to 
create any significant hydro issues in our area. With that said,
now may be a good time to ensure storm drains are clear of any 
leaves or other debris to prevent the back up and ponding of 
water from inefficient drainage in low lying areas.

As mentioned above, there will  be a powerful low level jet 
traversing the area from south to north Thursday afternoon and 
evening. GFS boundary layer winds are progged to peak between 35-45 
kts across the east facing higher slopes of the Poconos and 
Catskills. Confidence is increasing that this wind energy will 
translate to surface winds between 20-30 mph, with some 
occasional higher gusts certainly possible. In fact, if there 
is any mixing of the air in the boundary layer, even only up to 
950mb (1,000 ft agl) then gusts of 40-45 kts would be possible.
The most likely locations to see those higher gusts appears to 
be across eastern Luzerne, eastern Lackawanna, Southern Wayne, 
Pike and Sullivan NY counties. Will hold off on any wind 
advisories at this time and allow the next shift to evaluate the
latest model data tonight. Will mention in HWO.

Heading into Friday, the mid level dry slot is over the area in the 
early morning, but more moisture begins to shift into the forecast 
area from the west and southwest as the 700/500mb low moves in from 
PA through the day. Cooler temperatures aloft (-4C at 850mb) arrive 
later in the afternoon and evening. It will take some time for the 
surface temperatures to cool though. Expected scattered to numerous 
rain showers developing under the upper level low to impact the 
area, eventually mixing with and changing to some wet snow showers 
(over the higher elevations) later in the day and into Friday night. 
Little to no snow accumulation is expected due to the relatively 
mild temperatures. Overnight lows Friday night only dip down into 
the low to mid-30s, with most locations hovering just above freezing.

Heading into the weekend, there will be a few lingering lake effect 
rain (and maybe wet snow) showers up north on Saturday. Sunday is 
looking mainly dry and seasonably mild. A low passed by to our north 
and west Sunday night, with a cold front pushing through. This will 
open the door to more lake effect rain and maybe snow showers early 
next week, especially on Monday.
